newsitem.title: UK: GATT could spark more C sugar output cuts - analyst.
newsitem.headline: GATT could spark more C sugar output cuts - analyst.

text.p: The European Union (EU) could have to deepen production cuts of non-quota exportable sugar as its GATT commitments bite next century, a F.O. Licht analyst said on Thursday.
Under GATT, the EU must cut the amount of its sugar exports for which refunds are paid net of a quantity equivalent to preferential imports.
Of this net export volume the EU is committed to reduce 21 percent of the volume of exports and 36 percent of the cost.

Speaking at a two-day London conference hosted by Agra Europe, Licht's Christoph Berg said shipments would have to fall by only 340,000 tonnes to comply with the GATT commitments, as compared with the base period.
"One should not underestimate the knock-on effect which might be triggered by this reduction," he said.
Production within the export quota would become less attractive due to the reduced export refunds.
Production of "C" sugar -- produced over and above EU member states' quota -- could also become less attractive, depending on the cost structure of individual manufacturers, he said.
But the EU shipped between 4.5 and 5.0 million tonnes annually in recent years and would remain a big producer and exporter, although its export markets were likely to decline, Berg said.
"Change is imminent and many in the industry fear that a more liberal trading environment will lead to a massive loss of export markets," he said.
GATT restrictions would also affect the EU's sugar import market.
Variable import duties have to be replaced by fixed tariffs for agricultural products, with these tariffs to be reduced by 21 percent by 2001.

"The level of protection is bound to fall as the fixed duty comes down and there is a good chance that towards the end of this century, sugar could be imported economically in some of the higher-priced parts of the EU," Berg said.
